'''''Ammophila arenaria''''' (syn ''Calamagrostis arenaria''<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Peterson |first=Paul M. |last2=Soreng |first2=Robert J. |last3=Romaschenko |first3=Konstantin |last4=Barberá |first4=Patricia |last5=Quintanar |first5=Alejandro |last6=Aedo |first6=Carlos |last7=Saarela |first7=Jeffery M. |date=2022 |title=Phylogeny and biogeography of Calamagrostis (Poaceae: Pooideae: Poeae: Agrostidinae), description of a new genus, Condilorachia (Calothecinae), and expansion of Greeneochloa and Pentapogon (Echinopogoninae) |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/jse.12819 |journal=Journal of Systematics and Evolution |language=en |volume=60 |issue=3 |pages=570–590 |doi=10.1111/jse.12819 |issn=1759-6831|url-access=subscription }}</ref>) is a species of grass in the family [[Poaceae]]. It is known by the common names '''marram grass''' and '''European beachgrass'''.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ammophila arenaria |url=https://www.cal-ipc.org/plants/profile/ammophila-arenaria-profile/ |website=California Invasive Plant Council |access-date=15 March 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=David Chapman |title=Exploring the Cornish Coast |date=2008 |publisher=Alison Hodge |location=[[Penzance]] |isbn=9780906720561 |page=52}}</ref> It is one of two species of the genus ''[[Ammophila (Poaceae)|Ammophila]]''. It is native to the coastlines of Europe and North Africa where it grows in the sands of beach dunes. It is a perennial grass forming stiff, hardy clumps of erect stems up to {{convert|1.2|m|ft}} in height. It grows from a network of thick [[rhizome]]s which give it a sturdy anchor in its sand substrate and allow it to spread upward as sand accumulates. These rhizomes can grow laterally by {{convert|2|m|0}} in six months. One clump can produce 100 new shoots annually.<ref>{{cite web|title=Invasive Plants of California's Wildland: ''Ammophila arenaria'' |last=Apteker |first=Rachel |publisher=California Invasive Plants Council |url=http://www.cal-ipc.org/ip/management/ipcw/pages/detailreport.cfm@usernumber=5&surveynumber=182.php |access-date=2008-09-18}}</ref>

The rhizomes tolerate submersion in sea water and can break off and float in the currents to establish the grass at new sites.<ref name=UC/> The leaves are up to {{convert|1|m|ftin}} long and sharply pointed. The cylindrical [[inflorescence]] is up to {{convert|30|cm|in}} long. It is adapted to habitat made up of shifting, accreting sand layers, as well as that composed of [[Sand dune stabilization|stabilised dunes]].<ref name=UC/>

==Life cycle/phenology==
[[File:European Marram Grass (Ammophila arenaria) rolled leaf close-up.jpg|thumb|A single leaf of marram grass, showing the rolled leaf which reduces water loss]]
[[File:Ammophila arenaria leaf cross section.jpg|thumb|100x magnified cross section of a curled leaf]]
''Ammophila arenaria'' is a perennial plant, which means it can live for many years. It mainly grows in spring when leaf production exceeds leaf senescence. However, the conditions in autumn cause the plant to nearly stop growth while its leaves become aged.<ref>[http://eol.org/pages/1114196/details Encyclopedia of Life], 2015, ''Ammophila arenaria''.</ref> In winter, because of the cold temperatures, growth is very slow but does not stop.<ref name="Huiskes, A. H. L. 1979">Huiskes, A. H. L. (1979). ''Ammophila arenaria'' (L.) Link (''Psamma arenaria'' (L.) Roem. et Schult.; ''Calamgrostis arenaria'' (L.) Roth). The Journal of Ecology, 363-382.</ref>
As a [[xerophytic]] adaptation, its leaves curl during drought (see pictures). The relatively high humidity within the curled leaf prevents a rapid water loss. This is facilitated by the [[bulliform cell]]s located at the base of the V-shaped notch which swells and makes the leaf uncurl when filled with water.<ref name="lima_Leav">{{Cite web |title=Leaves and Leaf Anatomy |last=Norris |first=Ryan |work=Biology Microscopy |date= |access-date=13 May 2021 |publisher=The Ohio State University at Lima |url= https://lima.osu.edu/academics/departments/biology/plant-anatomy/leaves.html}}</ref>

This plant is highly adaptive in sand, and can withstand burial for more than one year. Unlike other plants which will die in sand, marram grass will elongate its leaves when it is buried by sand.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Maun|first1=M. A.|last2=Lapierre|first2=J.|date=1984|title=The Effects of Burial by Sand on ''Ammophila Breviligulata''|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2259534|journal=Journal of Ecology|volume=72|issue=3|pages=827–839|doi=10.2307/2259534|jstor=2259534|bibcode=1984JEcol..72..827M |issn=0022-0477|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=Ranwell>{{cite journal |author=Ranwell, D. |date=1960 |title=Newborough Warren, Anglesey: II. Plant associes and succession cycles of the sand dune and dune slack vegetation |journal=The Journal of Ecology |volume=48 |issue=1 |pages=117–141 |doi=10.2307/2257311 |jstor=2257311 |bibcode=1960JEcol..48..117R }}</ref>

Its inflorescences are initiated in autumn of the second year after germination and mature in May or June, and flowers are produced from May to August.<ref name="Huiskes, A. H. L. 1979"/><ref>Russo, M., Pickart, A., Morse, L., & Young, R. (1988). ELEMENT STEWARDSHIP ABSTRACT for ''Ammophila arenaria''.</ref> The fruit is mature by September, and the seeds germinate the next spring. Though the adult plant is strong, the seeds have low viability, and the seedlings also have low survival rates as well because of desiccation, burial, and erosion.<ref name="Encyclopedia of Life, 2015, ''Ammophila arenaria''.">content</ref> The main organ for its reproduction is rhizomes, which are dispersed along the shore by wind and water.<ref>Wallén, B. (1980). Changes in structure and function of ''Ammophila'' during primary succession. Oikos, 227-238</ref>

== Geographic distribution and habitat ==
[[File:European Marram Grass (Ammophila arenaria) growing on sand dunes in Wales 06.jpg|thumb|Sand dunes densely covered by marram grass at [[Oxwich Bay]], Wales]]

=== Natural global range ===
''Ammophila arenaria'' is a European and North African native plant. It occurs in Australia, Canada, Chile, Falkland Islands (Malvinas) (sub-Antarctic), New Zealand, South Africa and United States.<ref>{{cite web|title=''Ammophila arenaria''|url=http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=1518&fr=1&sts=sss&lang=EN|website=Global Invasive Species Database|access-date=4 May 2015}}</ref> In the Northern Hemisphere, it grows between 30 and 63 degrees north latitude.<ref name="Gadgil 2006">{{cite book |last1=Gadgil |first1=Ruth L. |url=https://ref.coastalrestorationtrust.org.nz/documents/marram-grass-friend-or-foe-a-review-of-the-use-of-ammophila-arenaria-on-new-zealand-sand-dunes/ |title=Marram Grass — Friend or Foe? A Review of the Use of ''Ammophila arenaria'' on New Zealand Sand Dunes |date=2006 |publisher=New Zealand Forest Research Institute Limited |series=Coastal Dune Vegetation Network Technical Bulletin |volume=5 |location=Rotorua |pages=32 pp |no-pp=y}}</ref> 

=== New Zealand range ===
Usually occurs on sand dunes, sometimes in inland sites with low fertility.<ref>{{cite web|title=''Ammophila arenaria''|url=http://nzpcn.org.nz/flora_details.aspx?ID=2521 |website=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |access-date=4 May 2015}}</ref> It occurs across the North and South Islands, and the Chatham Islands.

=== Habitat preferences ===
Marram grass grows on coastal sand dunes all over the world. It prefers growing on the active sand area and the windward side of the foredune. It prefers well-drained soils with different kinds of mineral compositions and low in organic matter. The optimal soil conditions for marram grass is a soil pH from 4.5 to 9.0, soil temperatures from {{convert|10-40|C|0}},<ref>Ranwell, D. (1959). Newborough Warren, Anglesey. I. The dune system and dune slack habitat. J. Ecology. 47(3), pp.571-601</ref> and salt concentrations of no more than 1.0–1.5%.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Pickart|first1=Andrea J|title= Control of European Beachgrass (''Ammophila arenaria'') on the West Coast of the United States|date=1997|publisher=. The Nature Conservancy Lanphere-Christensen Dunes Preserve Arcata|page=CA 95521}}</ref> Marram grass can also be found on alkaline soils with a high pH of around 9.1 and also acidic soils with pH less than 4.5. Adult plants can tolerate a large range of chemical issues. Marram grass has an ability to adapt dry sand well. Its leaves become rolled and tight when moisture levels are low.<ref name="Gadgil 2006"/>

===Invasiveness: Pacific coast of North America===
''A. arenaria'' is one of the most problematic [[noxious weeds]] of coastal [[California]]. This sand-adapted grass was [[introduced species|introduced]] to the beaches of western North America during the mid-19th century to stabilize shifting [[Dune|sand dune]]s. It grew readily, and it can now be found from California to [[British Columbia]]. The grass is invasive in the local ecosystems, forming dense monotypic stands that crowd out native vegetation, reduce [[biodiversity|species diversity]] of native [[arthropod]]s, and cover vital open stretches of sand used for nesting by the threatened western snowy plover (''[[Anarhynchus nivosus]]'').<ref name=UC>{{cite web |title=UC Cooperative Extension Species Profile: ''Ammophila arenaria'' |publisher=University of California |url=http://ucce.ucdavis.edu/datastore/detailreport.cfm?usernumber=5&surveynumber=182 |access-date=2008-09-18}}</ref> The plant's spread has changed the topography of some California beach ecosystems, especially in sand dunes. The presence of this grass was a major cause of the destruction of native dune habitat in [[Oregon]] and [[Washington (U.S. state)|Washington]] during the 20th century,<ref name="Pickart">{{cite web|url=https://www.cal-ipc.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/1997_symposium_proceedings1934.pdf|title=Control of European Beachgrass (''Ammophila arenaria'') on the West Coast of the United States|last=Pickart|first=Andrea J.|year=1997|work=1997 Symposium of the California Exotic Pest Plant Council|access-date=2008-09-20}}</ref> where it was planted precisely for its dune-stabilizing effect.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.opb.org/television/programs/ofg/segment/exploring-the-oregon-dunes/ |title=Exploring the Oregon Dunes . TV {{!}} OPB |website=www.opb.org |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170410083530/http://www.opb.org/television/programs/ofg/segment/exploring-the-oregon-dunes/ |archive-date=2017-04-10}}</ref>

Several methods have been employed in attempts to eradicate the grass in California, including manual pulling, burning, mechanical removal followed by saltwater irrigation, and [[glyphosate]] application.<ref name=Pickart/> Studies to find the best methods are ongoing; however, low-intensity treatments such as herbicides and manual pulling are being recommended by some researchers over mechanical treatments such as bulldozing due to potential negative impacts on endemic dune plants and dune geomorphology.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zarnetske |first=Phoebe |last2=Seabloom |first2=Eric |last3=Hacker |first3=Sally |date=November 24, 2010 |title=Non-target effects of invasive species management: beachgrass, birds, and bulldozers in coastal dunes |url=https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1890/ES10-00101.1 |journal=Ecosphere |volume=1 |issue=5 |pages=1-20 |doi=10.1890/ES10-00101.1 |via=Wiley Online Library|doi-access=free }}</ref>

The California Conservation Corps has made major efforts in the removal of the invasive beachgrass, such as an initiative at [[Morro Strand State Beach]] in 2000.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Beach Grass Removal Project |url=https://www.parks.ca.gov/?page_id=21575 |access-date=November 7, 2024 |website=California Department of Parks and Recreation}}</ref>

=== Invasiveness: New Zealand and Australia ===
Not only is it invasive in California, it is also a highly invasive weed in coastal areas of New Zealand and Western Australia, where it was introduced for the same purpose in California, to stabilise dunes, outcompeting native [[Spinifex (coastal grass)|''Spinifex'']] species. It is named in the Department of Conservation's 2024 list of environmental weeds. However, in New Zealand the larvae of the endemic moth species ''[[Agrotis innominata]]'' has adapted to using ''A. arenaria'' as one of its main host species.<ref name="Patrick & Green">{{Cite Q|Q105740814|pages=32–36}}</ref> It has been suggested that prior to the removal of this invasive grass from the coasts of New Zealand, surveys be undertaken to establish whether this endemic moth is present in order to assist with the conservation of that species.<ref name="Patrick & Green" />

==Predators, parasites, and diseases==
Marram grass does not carry any major disease in New Zealand, as only three pathogenic fungi (''Claviceps purpurea'', ''Uredo'' sp. and ''Colletotrichum graminicola'') are present on the island. These three fungi result in ergot, rust and leaf spot, respectively, and are found both on flower-heads and leaves. However, in European countries, there are many pests known to feed on marram grass. Those pests can kill 30–40% of the tillers, and also damage other species. The fungi, always found in soil, may decrease vigour on stabilized sand.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Gadgil|first1=Ruth L. |year=2002 |title=Marram gass (''Ammophila arenaria'') and coastal sand stability in New Zealand |journal=New Zealand Journal of Forestry Science |volume=32 |issue=2 |pages=165–180 |url=https://ref.coastalrestorationtrust.org.nz/site/assets/files/3126/gadgil_r_2001_marramgrassammophilaarenaariaandcoastalsandstability.pdf }}</ref>

==Uses==
The roots of marram grass are edible, although thin and fibrous. The flowering stems and leaves are used for thatching, basketry and making brooms. Fiber from the stem is used for making paper, and the rhizomes are used for making rope and mats.<ref>Plant For A Future. (n.d.). ''Ammophila arenaria'' - (L.)Link. Retrieved from http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Ammophila+arenaria</ref>
